claims.claim: For every fixed threshold τ≥2, a simple three-occurrence color sequence encodes a spanning forest with exactly two roots, even root degrees, and odd nonroot degrees.
claims.evidence: Let N=2n and q=n−1. In any play empty after the prefix, the first two height-(τ−1) copies of a color cannot be adjacent: they would vanish because 2(τ−1)≥τ, stranding the sole remaining copy. Thus the first 2q moves leave N−2 distinct occupied vertices and exactly two vacancies. A final copy must be adjacent to both earlier copies; adjacency to fewer leaves at least one copy permanently present. Direct the two resulting graph edges from the vacant center to the cleared vertices. Assign an initial vacancy time before all clearing moves and each other vertex its unique clearing time. Every directed edge goes from a vertex with earlier vacancy time to vertices with later clearing time, excluding cycles. Every nonroot is cleared exactly once and hence has one parent; the N−2 edges therefore form two rooted spanning-tree components. Each use of a center adds two children, so every root has even degree and every nonroot has one parent plus an even number of children, hence odd degree.
claims.search_method: General invariant and temporal-order proof, supplemented by deterministic exhaustive enumeration of every simple graph on 2, 4, and 6 vertices and all 368738 successful abstract clearing schedules, using integer bit masks only.

claims.claim: For the leaf-corona G of a connected subcubic graph H, the above prefix can empty G if and only if H has a Hamiltonian path.
claims.evidence: Soundness follows from the parity forest. A pendant leaf that is a root is isolated, while every nonroot pendant leaf has its unique edge in the forest. For |V(H)|≥2, both roots cannot be pendant leaves because the forest has exactly two components. If neither is pendant, deleting every pendant edge leaves two forest components in H, each with its root as its unique odd-degree vertex, contradicting handshaking componentwise. Hence exactly one root is a pendant a′ and is an isolated component; the other root r is original. Removing all pendant vertices from the other component yields a spanning tree T⊆H. If r=a, every degree in the nontrivial tree T is even, impossible. Otherwise precisely a and r have odd degree in T. Since H is subcubic, every other vertex of T has positive even degree exactly two; the tree degree sum then gives deg_T(a)+deg_T(r)=2, so both equal one and T is a Hamiltonian path. Conversely, for a Hamiltonian path v1,…,vn, take roots v1′ and vn; pair color ci on v_{n−i+1}′ and v_{n−i}, then use centers vn,v_{n−1},…,v2 in final-color order. Every center is vacant when needed and clears its pair. The n=1 case has an empty prefix and is directly equivalent.
claims.search_method: General leaf-degree, componentwise handshaking, and tree degree-sum proof; exhaustive comparison of Hamiltonian-path existence with parity-forest existence for all 516 connected labeled subcubic graphs of orders 1 through 5; literal Hexasort simulation for 129 graph/threshold cases through order 4 and thresholds 2, 3, and 4.

claims.claim: Fitting Hexasort is NP-hard for every exact fixed threshold τ≥2, even on graphs of maximum degree four.
claims.evidence: Use Hamiltonian Path on connected subcubic graphs. The leaf-corona construction is polynomial and has maximum degree at most four. By claim 1, its prefix leaves the N-vertex board empty exactly when the source graph has a Hamiltonian path. Append N single height-one stacks whose colors are pairwise fresh and absent from the prefix. For τ≥2 none can vanish or interact with any other stack, so each irreversibly consumes one currently empty vertex. Consequently all N suffix moves fit exactly when all N vertices were vacant after the prefix. This is a many-one equivalence for every fixed τ, using only the constant heights τ−1 and 1.
claims.search_method: Direct audit of source problem, polynomial construction, degree bound, and both reduction directions; integer-only exhaustive suffix accounting for every board size 1 through 64 and every possible initial occupancy, totaling 2144 cases.

claims.claim: Complete classification: the constant-threshold problem is NP-complete for every fixed τ≥2, while τ=1 is trivial.
claims.evidence: A certificate specifies one vertex per stack and has polynomial length; legality and all same-color neighbor merges can be simulated with polynomially many exact integer operations, proving membership in NP. Claim 2 supplies NP-hardness for every exact fixed τ≥2. For a language promised t≤T with any fixed T≥2, the exact-t=2 instances form an NP-hard subfamily, while the language remains in NP. At t=1, every allowed stack has positive height and therefore vanishes immediately upon placement; the board remains empty after every legal move. Thus every sequence fits on a nonempty graph, while on an empty graph precisely the empty sequence fits, which is trivial to decide.
claims.search_method: Certificate-verification analysis combined with the fixed-threshold reduction; deterministic integer checks of 297 threshold-one boundary cases and the exact simulations and suffix checks reported for claims 1 and 2.

target_evidence: The exact target requests a complexity classification for Fitting Hexasort when t is bounded by a fixed constant. The draft proves the stronger pointwise statement that every exact fixed threshold τ≥2 is NP-complete and separately handles τ=1. It also explicitly derives the bounded-promise formulation: for every fixed upper bound T≥2, instances with t≤T are NP-complete because the restriction contains the NP-hard exact-t=2 subfamily and lies in NP; T=1 is trivial. The reduction is polynomial, preserves a fixed threshold, and proves an if-and-only-if rather than a merely necessary condition. Therefore the full target, at its requested strength, is established, and the draft's claimed_resolution of FULL is ACCURATE.
